identity.name: Jungian Model of the Psyche
identity.label: Jungian Analytical Psychology
identity.description: A theoretical model of the human psyche associated with Carl Gustav Jung. The model describes consciousness, the personal unconscious, the collective unconscious, archetypal patterns, psychic functions, psychological orientations, complexes, symbolic processes, projection, compensation, individuation and relationships between conscious and unconscious psychological contents. The objects and processes represented here are constructs within Jungian analytical psychology. Their presence in this model does not by itself assert that each construct constitutes an independently established empirical mechanism.

identity.name: Jungian Psyche
identity.description: The total psychological field represented by the Jungian model, including conscious and unconscious processes and structures.

identity.name: Consciousness
identity.description: The field of psychic contents that are currently available to awareness and related to the conscious standpoint of the individual.

identity.name: Ego
identity.description: The center of the field of consciousness and the organizing reference point through which conscious identity, continuity, attention and intentional experience are represented in Jungian psychology.
A perception, thought, feeling, memory, image, representation or other psychic content currently available to consciousness.
Selective allocation of conscious awareness toward particular psychic contents, objects or processes.
The theoretical domain of personally acquired psychic contents that are not currently conscious, including forgotten, repressed or insufficiently differentiated material and complexes.
Experiences belonging to the individual's personal history and contributing to the organization of personal psychic contents.
Representations associated with personally experienced events, information and situations.
Personal psychic material represented within Jungian theory as excluded or insufficiently accessible to ordinary conscious awareness.
A theoretical layer of the Jungian psyche associated with archetypal patterns and potentials that are not understood as being derived solely from an individual's personal history.
The system of archetypal patterns represented within Jungian analytical psychology.
A recurring structural pattern in Jungian theory capable of organizing perception, imagination, affect, interpretation and symbolic experience.
The archetypal representation of psychic totality and a central organizing principle of the psyche within Jungian analytical psychology.
A psychological structure associated with the social role, social presentation and adaptation of the individual to interpersonal and cultural expectations.
A Jungian archetypal concept associated with aspects of personality that are insufficiently recognized, accepted or integrated by consciousness.
A Jungian archetypal concept concerning an unconscious psychic figure historically described by Jung as an inner feminine image in a man's psyche.
A Jungian archetypal concept concerning an unconscious psychic figure historically described by Jung as an inner masculine image in a woman's psyche.
An archetypal pattern associated with overcoming obstacles, differentiation, initiative and conscious agency in symbolic narratives.
An archetypal symbolic pattern associated with potentiality, renewal, emergence and development.
An archetypal symbolic pattern associated with maternal containment, nourishment, origin, protection and dependency.
An archetypal symbolic pattern associated with authority, order, law, structure and guidance.
An archetypal symbolic pattern associated with contradiction, disruption, ambiguity, transformation and destabilization of established patterns.
An archetypal symbolic pattern associated with knowledge, guidance, insight and orientation.
An archetypal symbolic pattern associated with wisdom, intuition, guidance and transformation.
An archetypal pattern associated with origin, containment, nourishment, fertility, protection and potentially overwhelming dependency.
The four principal psychological functions described in Jung's typological model: thinking, feeling, sensation and intuition.
A Jungian psychological function concerned with conceptual differentiation, classification, logical relations and judgment through ideas.
A Jungian psychological function concerned with valuation, significance, preference and appraisal of psychological value.
A Jungian psychological function concerned with perception of concrete actuality and qualities of directly experienced situations.
A Jungian psychological function concerned with perception of possibilities, implicit relationships, emerging patterns and meanings not necessarily derived from direct sensory observation.
The Jungian distinction between introversion and extraversion as orientations of psychic energy, attention and valuation.
An orientation in which psychic attention and valuation are primarily directed toward subjective experience and the inner psychological world.
An orientation in which psychic attention and valuation are primarily directed toward objects, situations and the external environment.
A system of emotionally charged associations and psychologically related contents organized around recurring personal themes.
An organized cluster of emotionally charged memories, representations, expectations, perceptions and behavioral tendencies associated around a psychological theme.
A memory associated with the thematic and affective organization of a psychological complex.
A representation, image, belief or association organized around the theme of a complex.
An expectation or anticipatory pattern associated with a psychological complex.
A system of symbolic experiences and representations through which psychological contents may be expressed or related to consciousness.
A symbolic representation whose psychological meaning is not exhausted by its immediately apparent literal or conceptual interpretation.
A symbolic psychological experience occurring during sleep that may contain images, affects, narratives and transformations of psychic material.
A culturally transmitted symbolic narrative that can express recurring archetypal themes and psychological meanings.
An imaginative psychic experience involving internally generated images, narratives, scenarios or possibilities.
A Jungian method of engaging consciously with spontaneously emerging images, fantasies and unconscious material while maintaining conscious psychological observation.
The dynamic relationships and processes through which conscious and unconscious psychological contents influence, compensate, conflict, activate and transform one another.
A psychological process in which psychic contents associated with the subject are experienced as belonging to another person, object or situation.
A theoretical process in which unconscious activity complements or compensates for one-sidedness in a conscious psychological attitude.
A psychological process in which the ego or another psychic structure becomes strongly aligned with a role, image, group, object or psychic content.
A process through which previously undifferentiated psychological contents, functions or structures become more distinct and recognizable.
A process through which differentiated psychic contents become related within a more coherent psychological organization.
A process through which a previously latent psychic structure or content becomes psychologically active.
A Jungian term for the activation of a particular psychic complex or configuration in response to a situation, stimulus or psychological condition.

A developmental process in Jungian psychology through which differentiated and previously unconscious aspects of the psyche become increasingly related within a more integrated psychological totality.
A process of becoming consciously related to aspects of personality represented by the Shadow and establishing a more differentiated relationship with them.
The psychological relationship between the conscious ego and the archetypal Self within Jungian theory.
Psychic content that is not currently within ordinary conscious awareness in the Jungian model.
An event, perception, association, memory or situation capable of activating a previously latent psychological configuration or complex.
The interpersonal, cultural and social environment within which the individual performs roles and establishes relationships.
A state in which psychic content is available to conscious awareness.
A state in which psychic content is not currently available to ordinary conscious awareness.
A relatively inactive psychological configuration capable of becoming activated.
A psychological configuration that is currently active and influencing experience.
A psychological configuration with unusually strong influence over current experience.
A state in which psychological contents are becoming related to conscious organization.
A state in which a psychological content or structure has become more coherently related to the psyche.
A state associated with an ongoing developmental psychological process.
The current configuration of conscious and unconscious psychological contents represented by the model.
Transformation from a latent psychic configuration to an activated configuration.
Transformation through which previously undifferentiated psychological contents become more distinct and consciously recognizable.
Transformation through which differentiated psychological contents become more coherently related within the psyche.

notes.note: Archetypes are represented as theoretical psychic structures rather than as concrete physical objects.
The distinction between personal and collective unconscious belongs to the conceptual architecture of Jungian theory.
Thinking, Feeling, Sensation and Intuition are represented as functions rather than anatomical structures.
Introversion and Extraversion are represented as orientations rather than fixed personality objects.
Projection, Compensation, Differentiation and Integration are represented as psychic processes.
Individuation is represented as a developmental transformation involving relationships among multiple psychic structures.
Dreams, symbols, myths, fantasies and active imagination are represented as symbolic objects or processes connecting psychological contents and representations.
